guides.seoTitle: Best stick vacuum 2026: 22 models tested | HouseholdMe
guides.intro: After six weeks of testing 22 models on hardwood, carpet and the stairs, we recommend the Vorta S9: strong enough for a whole house, light enough to carry up the stairs.
guides.photoNote: stick vacuums in the test house
guides.forWho: A stick vacuum is handy when you want to do a quick clean without a cord. In an apartment or small house it can fully replace your canister vacuum. If you have a lot of shag carpet or a home larger than about 1,300 sq ft, we recommend a stick vacuum as a second machine next to a canister model.
guides.howTested: Each model picked up three standardized dirt mixes on hardwood, low-pile and high-pile carpet. We weighed the debris collected, measured the actual runtime on the lowest and highest settings, and recorded the noise level at one meter.
guides.howCaption: Sarah weighs the collected sand after every test round. Photo: HouseholdMe
guides.bought: We bought 18 of the 22 machines ourselves; four were loaned by the manufacturer and returned after testing.
guides.tableNote: Pickup: percentage of test dirt collected, averaged over three floor types. Runtime on standard setting. Noise at 1 meter.

faq.q: Can a stick vacuum replace my regular vacuum?
faq.a: In a home up to about 1,300 sq ft with mostly hard floors, yes. With a lot of shag carpet, a canister vacuum still cleans more thoroughly.

faq.q: How long does the battery last?
faq.a: Expect three to five years. Ideally, choose a model whose battery you can replace yourself.

faq.q: Is a more expensive model always better?
faq.a: No. Above $400 we mostly saw extra accessories and a display, not necessarily better cleaning results.

faq.q: Do manufacturers have influence on this guide?
faq.a: No. Manufacturers cannot pay for a spot and only see our conclusions after publication.

faq.q: Which is better, a stick vacuum or a canister vacuum?
faq.a: A canister vacuum still cleans high-pile carpet more thoroughly and has no battery that wears out. A stick vacuum is quicker to grab, easier on the stairs and takes up less space. For most homes with hard floors, a good stick vacuum is enough.

faq.q: How many watts should a good stick vacuum have?
faq.a: Wattage says little about how well it cleans. In our test, a model with fewer air watts picked up more dirt than a stronger model because its brush worked better. Look at test results per floor type.

faq.q: Can I vacuum the stairs with a stick vacuum?
faq.a: Yes, and that's exactly where they shine. Remove the wand and use the unit as a handheld with the small turbo brush. A model under 2.5 kilos is the most comfortable.

faq.q: Is a stick vacuum good for pet hair?
faq.a: Yes, if it has a brush that doesn't let hair wrap around it. The Northwind X2 did this best in our test. With other models you need to cut the brush clean regularly.

faq.q: How often should I clean the filter?
faq.a: Rinse a washable filter once a month and let it dry for a day. Replace it once a year. If you have pets, clean it every two weeks.

faq.q: How much electricity does a stick vacuum use?
faq.a: A full charge uses 0.05 to 0.1 kWh. If you charge it every day, that costs roughly $5 to $10 a year.

faq.q: Can a stick vacuum stay on the charger all the time?
faq.a: Yes. Modern batteries stop charging when they're full. A battery does last longer if you store it at room temperature.

faq.q: When is a stick vacuum cheapest?
faq.a: Prices usually drop around Black Friday in November and in January. In our price history, the Vorta S9 dropped by up to 15 percent during those periods last year.

summary: Best pick for most people: the Vorta S9. It picked up 96 percent of our test dirt, runs for 48 minutes and at 2.4 kilos is light enough to carry up the stairs.
Best budget pick: the Kleen Air 300. Fine on hard floors in an apartment, but the battery is empty after 35 minutes.
Best upgrade: the Northwind X2. The highest pickup on high-pile carpet, two swappable batteries and a brush that long hair doesn't wrap around.

body: In our test, the Vorta S9 was the stick vacuum that most often did exactly what we expected. On hardwood it picked up 99 percent of the test dirt, on low-pile carpet 97 percent and on high-pile carpet still 92 percent. Only the Northwind X2, which costs over $200 more, did better.

At 2.4 kilos it isn't the lightest, but the weight sits low in the hand. That makes it feel lighter than the Kleen Air 300 when you vacuum under the couch or along the ceiling. Sarah did a fourteen-step staircase with it without resting her arm.

On the standard setting we got 48 minutes. That's enough for a single-family home of around 1,100 sq ft in one go, including the stairs. On turbo, that drops to 11 minutes. You only use that setting for a dirty doormat or the car.

You empty the 0.6-liter bin with a slider that pushes the dirt out, so you don't have to put your fingers in the dust. The HEPA filter is washable. After six weeks of daily use we noticed no loss of suction.

There are two downsides. The wall mount has to be screwed in, because there's no freestanding dock. And with long hair, the brush clogs faster than the Northwind's. If you have a dog with a long coat, you'll need to cut the brush free about once a week.
deep.bestFor: you want one vacuum for a home up to about 1,300 sq ft with a mix of hard floors and low-pile carpet.

body: The Kleen Air 300 costs half as much as our top pick, and you notice, but less than you'd think. On hardwood and tile it picked up 98 percent, almost as much as the Vorta. On carpet that dropped to 90 percent on low-pile and 79 percent on high-pile.
At 2.2 kilos it's the lightest of our picks. It's narrow enough to fit between the legs of a dining chair, and the floor head has LED lights that make crumbs and hair visible on a dark floor.

The battery is its weak point. After 35 minutes on the standard setting it's empty, and charging takes four hours. A second battery costs $39 and clicks in within seconds. For an apartment up to 750 sq ft you probably won't need one.
It's also the loudest machine among our picks: 74 dB at one meter. That's about the level of a hair dryer. If that doesn't bother you, you get a lot of vacuum for little money.
deep.bestFor: you live in an apartment with mostly hard floors and don't want to spend more than $200.

body: The Northwind X2 is the best stick vacuum we tested this year. It picked up 98 percent of the test dirt on average, and 95 percent on high-pile carpet. That's better than several canister vacuums we tested earlier.

The brush has combs that cut long hair and guide it to the bin. After vacuuming up 20 grams of dog hair, nothing was wrapped around the Northwind's roller. The Vorta had 1.8 grams, the Kleen Air 3.4 grams.
It comes with two batteries that each last 62 minutes. While you use one, the other charges in a separate charger. So in a big house you never have to stop halfway.

At 2.7 kilos it's the heaviest. For picking up a few crumbs every day, that's more vacuum than you need. The difference with the Vorta is $210. You mainly pay for better results on carpet, less hassle with hair and the second battery.
deep.bestFor: you have a lot of carpet, long-haired pets or a home larger than 1,300 sq ft.

full.buyIntro: A stick vacuum costs between $80 and $900. The price says only so much about how well it cleans. In our experience, these seven points decide whether you'll still be happy with your purchase in three years.

buying.heading: Suction: look at test results, not watts
paragraphs: Manufacturers often list power in watts, or suction in air watts or pascals. Those numbers say little, because they're measured without a brush and without a floor. In our test, a model with 150 air watts picked up more dirt than one with 220 air watts, because its brush made better contact with the carpet.

More important is how the brush is built. A roller with stiff bristles works best on carpet. A soft felt or microfiber roller picks up fine dust on hard floors better. The best models have both, or a roller that combines the two.
buying.tip: Look for an independent test with results per floor type, like our results above.

buying.heading: Battery: runtime, charging time and replaceability
paragraphs: The runtime on the box almost always applies to the lowest setting without a spinning brush. On the setting you actually use, it's often half. That's why we list runtime on the standard setting with the floor head.
As a rule of thumb, you need about 25 minutes per 540 sq ft of floor. So for a 1,100 sq ft home with stairs, 45 minutes is comfortable.

Also check whether you can replace the battery yourself. A lithium-ion battery loses a noticeable part of its capacity after three to five years. If you can unclip it, you buy a new one for $40 to $80. If it's built in, the whole vacuum is done.
buying.tip: Before you buy, check whether the spare battery can be ordered from the manufacturer. If not, choose another model.

buying.heading: Weight and balance
paragraphs: Stick vacuums weigh between 2 and 3.2 kilos. Just as important is where that weight sits. A model with the motor and battery at the top, near your hand, feels heavy when you vacuum under furniture. A model with the weight low on the wand is nicer on the floor but more awkward as a handheld.
We had five testers of different heights each use every model for ten minutes. The Vorta S9 and the Kleen Air 300 got the best ratings. The heaviest models were ruled out by testers under 5'5".

buying.heading: Bin and filter
paragraphs: Most stick vacuums have a bin of 0.4 to 0.8 liters. A small bin isn't a problem as long as it's easy to empty. Check whether you can open it over the trash can without the dust swirling up, and without having to pull hair out.
If you suffer from dust mites or hay fever, choose a model with a HEPA filter and a sealed system. That way the vacuum doesn't blow fine dust back into the room from the back.

buying.heading: Noise
paragraphs: Stick vacuums produce between 65 and 80 dB at one meter. Every extra 3 dB doubles the sound energy, and 10 dB more sounds about twice as loud. So the difference between the Vorta S9 (69 dB) and the Hoverline 5 (76 dB) is clearly audible, especially when a baby is sleeping or you want to vacuum in the evening.

buying.heading: Accessories you'll actually use
paragraphs: Almost every stick vacuum comes with a crevice tool and a dusting brush. You'll use both. A small turbo brush is handy for the couch and the stairs, especially if you have pets. A wall mount with charging keeps your vacuum always ready.
In our experience, extra attachments for mattresses, curtains or the car mostly stay in the box. Don't let them be the deciding factor.

buying.heading: Smart features
paragraphs: More expensive models have a display, a dust sensor that adjusts suction automatically, or an app. We found the dust sensor useful: it extended the Northwind's runtime by about eight minutes, because it vacuums more gently on clean stretches of floor. An app adds little to a stick vacuum.

tiers.heading: Up to $200
tiers.text: Good on hard floors in a small home. Runtime is usually 25 to 35 minutes, noise is higher and the brush is simpler.

tiers.heading: $200 to $400
tiers.text: This is where you find the best value: good pickup on carpet, at least 40 minutes of runtime and a replaceable battery.

tiers.heading: Over $400
tiers.text: You pay for high-pile carpet, pet hair, a second battery and extras like a display. Only worth it if you really need them.

full.vsNote: Many households combine two machines. A robot keeps the floor tidy every day, a stick vacuum handles the stairs, the couch and the corners. A canister vacuum remains the best choice if your home is mostly high-pile carpet.

care.heading: Empty the bin after every use
care.text: A full bin reduces suction even before it reaches the max line. Ideally empty it outside or directly over the trash can.

care.heading: Rinse the filter once a month
care.text: Rinse washable filters under the tap, without soap. Let the filter dry for at least 24 hours. A damp filter will grow mold and smell.

care.heading: Remove hair from the brush
care.text: Take out the roller and cut hair loose with scissors along the groove. Do this weekly if you have pets.

care.heading: Don't store the battery empty or in the cold
care.text: Don't leave the vacuum for weeks with an empty battery, and don't keep it in a cold shed or garage. Below 40°F a battery loses capacity faster.

care.heading: Check the wand if suction drops
care.text: If it suddenly cleans worse, look inside the wand and the opening of the floor head. A sock or a Lego brick is the most common cause.

care.heading: Replace the filter once a year
care.text: Even a washable filter wears out. A new filter costs $10 to $25 and brings suction back to its original level.

durable: A stick vacuum consists of a battery, a motor and a lot of plastic. How long it lasts depends mainly on two things: can you replace the battery, and are parts like the brush and filter sold separately?

For our three picks, the battery, filter, brush roll and bin can be ordered separately from the manufacturer. Vorta says it guarantees parts availability for seven years, Northwind for ten. Kleen Air doesn't give a time frame.

Under US law, products come with an implied warranty that they'll work as reasonably expected, even beyond the manufacturer's warranty in many states. If a vacuum at this price fails within a few years, contact the retailer or manufacturer and ask about your options.
Is your old vacuum worn out? Take it to an electronics recycling drop-off or a participating retailer. Remove the battery first, because lithium batteries don't belong in household trash.

situations.heading: A home with stairs
situations.text: On the stairs, weight matters more than suction. You hold the machine with one hand and lift it a bit on every step. Under 2.5 kilos you'll barely notice it in your wrist after a full flight; above 2.8 kilos it gets heavy. Switch the stick vacuum to handheld mode with the small motorized brush for the stairs. The Vorta S9 and the Kleen Air 300 were the most comfortable in this test. The Northwind X2 worked too, but after three flights most testers wanted a break.

situations.heading: Pets
situations.text: Cat and dog hair wraps around the brush roll and reduces pickup. Choose a model with an anti-tangle brush or a roller with combs that loosen hair while vacuuming. Empty the bin after every use: pet hair fills the bin faster than sand or crumbs and gets in the way of the cyclone. In our test house, the Northwind X2 still ran without clogs after ten sessions in a home with a long-haired cat; with the Vorta S9 we had to clean the roller with scissors twice.

situations.heading: Allergies or asthma
situations.text: Look for a fully sealed system with a HEPA filter. A filter alone isn't enough: if there are seams in the housing, fine dust still escapes. Empty the bin outside or over a trash bag you tie shut immediately, and choose a model that lets you empty the bin without touching the dirt. Wash the filter on time, but then let it dry for at least 24 hours. A damp filter grows mold, which is worse for people with allergies than a dirty filter.

situations.heading: A small apartment
situations.text: In a home up to about 750 sq ft with hard floors, you don't need a top model. A runtime of 30 to 35 minutes on the standard setting is plenty for a full clean. Look mainly at storage: a model that can stand upright or has a no-drill wall mount fits more easily in a small hallway. The Kleen Air 300 is our pick here, because it's light and takes up little space.

situations.heading: A large home with carpet
situations.text: With more than 1,300 sq ft and a lot of carpet, you hit two limits: the battery and the bin. On the highest setting, almost no model gets more than 15 minutes. A swappable battery solves that, as does a second charging point upstairs. A bigger bin saves trips to the trash can. In this situation we recommend the Northwind X2, or the Vorta S9 with an extra battery.

situations.heading: Car and small jobs
situations.text: Most stick vacuums turn into a handheld with a few clicks. For the car you'll need a narrow nozzle and a small brush; almost all models include them in the box. Watch the weight of the handheld part alone: with the lightest models it's about 1.3 kilos, with the heaviest almost 2 kilos. You'll feel that difference after ten minutes of vacuuming under seats.

full.specsIntro: The box of a stick vacuum is full of numbers. Some of them say little about how well it works in your home. After 22 tests, this is what we think of the most important specs.

specsExplained.text: Motor power says little about suction on the floor. An efficient motor with good airflow and a smart brush often outperforms a heavier motor with poor design. In our test, a 350-watt model scored higher on carpet than a 450-watt model.

Air watts (AW) and pascals (Pa) indicate how much suction remains at the opening. That says more than watts, but manufacturers measure in different ways and often without a brush. Use these values only to compare models from the same brand.

The runtime on the box is almost always measured on the lowest setting without the motorized brush. Expect about half on the standard setting with the motorized brush, and a quarter on the highest setting. We always measure with the brush you actually use, on the setting you actually use.

Manufacturers list the total capacity of the bin, but you can only fill it to the max line. In practice, the usable capacity is 30 to 40 percent smaller. A 0.6-liter bin is enough for an average home without pets; with a dog or cat you'll want 0.75 liters or more.

A difference of 3 dB(A) already sounds noticeably louder, 10 dB(A) sounds about twice as loud. Below 70 dB(A) on the standard setting you can still talk while someone vacuums. Note: many manufacturers only list the noise on the lowest setting.

mistakes.heading: Using the highest setting by default
mistakes.text: On hard floors, the highest setting barely picks up more, while the battery drains three to four times faster. Only use boost on carpet or in corners where dirt is stuck.

mistakes.heading: Letting the bin get too full
mistakes.text: Above the max line, dirt ends up in the cyclone and the filter. Suction then drops quickly and the filter wears faster. Empty the bin after every use, even if it doesn't look full yet.

mistakes.heading: Putting the filter back wet
mistakes.text: A damp filter lets less air through, starts to smell and can damage the motor. Let it dry for at least a day after rinsing. Most brands sell a second filter separately for $15 to $25.

mistakes.heading: Charging in a cold shed or hot sun
mistakes.text: Lithium-ion batteries wear faster at temperatures below 40°F and above 95°F. Store and charge your stick vacuum indoors, ideally in a hallway or closet at room temperature.

mistakes.heading: Vacuuming up wet spills
mistakes.text: A regular stick vacuum isn't made for moisture. Wet coffee grounds or spilled milk clog the filter and can ruin the motor. Wipe up wet messes first, or choose a model with a separate wet function.

mistakes.heading: Leaving hair in the brush
mistakes.text: A roller full of hair doesn't sweep well anymore and strains the brush motor. Cut hair loose every few weeks. On most models the roller clicks out without tools.

verdict: For most households, the Vorta S9 is the best stick vacuum right now. In our test it picked up 96 percent of the test dirt, runs for 48 minutes on the standard setting and weighs 2.4 kilos. That makes it strong enough for a whole house and light enough for the stairs. The price is under $400, which is reasonable for this performance.

If you have a small apartment with mostly hard floors, the Kleen Air 300 is a good choice for about half the money. It's lighter and cheaper, but you give up runtime and carpet performance. If you live in a large home, have a lot of shag carpet or a long-haired pet, the Northwind X2 is worth the extra $200 for its swappable battery and anti-tangle brush.

Whichever you choose: when buying, look for a replaceable battery and separately available parts. A stick vacuum you can repair lasts longer and is cheaper in the long run than a cheap model you throw away after three years. We keep testing new models and will update this guide as soon as there's a better pick.

glossary.definition: A measure of airflow and vacuum combined. Manufacturers measure this in different ways, so you can't compare brands well.
The percentage of test dirt a vacuum picked up in our test. This is our most important measurement.
A filter that captures at least 99.95 percent of particles of 0.3 micrometers. Important for allergies or asthma.
A floor head with its own motor that spins the brush roll. Needed to beat dirt out of carpet.
A battery you can unclip and charge separately, so you can keep vacuuming with a second battery.
A system that spins the air so dirt is flung out of the airflow. As a result, suction drops less as the bin fills up.
Sound level, corrected for how the human ear perceives sound. 10 dB(A) more sounds about twice as loud.

questions.q: Does the Vorta S9 fit under a bed with 5 inches of clearance?
questions.a: Yes. The floor head is 3.3 inches tall and the wand can lie almost flat. We got under our 4.3-inch test bed.

questions.q: Can I mop with it too?
questions.a: No, the S9 has no mopping function. For vacuuming and mopping at the same time, we recommend a wet-dry vacuum.

faq.q: How long is the warranty?

faq.q: Can it handle drywall dust?
faq.a: For a little dust after drilling, yes. For large amounts we recommend a shop vac, because the filter clogs quickly.

guides.intro: We let 17 robot vacuums loose for five weeks in a home with a cat and a dog. The Robomop P7 picked up the most hair and got stuck the least.
guides.forWho: A robot vacuum keeps the floor clean every day without you having to think about it. With pets, that’s often the difference between a floor covered in hair and one that still looks tidy after a day.
guides.howTested: Each robot cleaned the ground floor of our test house twenty times. We counted how often it got stuck, measured how much pet hair it collected and checked how well the app kept track of the home map.

faq.q: Can a robot vacuum get over thresholds?
faq.a: Most models handle thresholds up to 2 centimeters. Our pick cleared 2.2-centimeter thresholds in the test.

faq.q: Do I need a self-empty station?
faq.a: With pets it’s handy: the robot empties itself and you only need to replace the bag about once a month.

picks.verdict: A simple robot that’s good enough for an apartment without thresholds.
pros: Low enough to fit under the couch
cons: Drives randomly instead of using a map

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: Robomop P9 Ultra
picks.verdict: Vacuums and mops, then cleans the mop pads itself with hot water.
pros: Best mopping result in the test
cons: High price and expensive replacement parts

guides.author: thomas
guides.title: The best air fryer for a family of four
guides.intro: We cooked more than 30 kilos of fries, chicken thighs and vegetables in 14 air fryers. The Aerolux Duo XL is big enough for a family and cooks the most evenly.
guides.forWho: An air fryer is handy when you want a quick meal without preheating the oven. For a family of four you need at least 5 liters of capacity, or two baskets.
guides.howTested: In each air fryer we cooked the same portions of frozen fries, fresh fries and chicken thighs. We measured core temperature, rated browning and tracked power use per cooking round.

faq.q: How much electricity does an air fryer use?
faq.a: In our test, a round of fries used 0.3 kWh on average, about half of an electric oven.

faq.q: Can I use parchment paper in an air fryer?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the food holds the paper in place. Loose paper can blow against the heating element.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: Aerolux Duo XL
picks.verdict: Two 4.5-liter baskets that finish at the same time, with the most even cooking result.

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: Crispa 4
picks.verdict: For one or two people, this small air fryer cooks just as crispy as models twice the price.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: Aerolux Pro Dual
picks.verdict: Has a built-in meat thermometer and a viewing window.
cons: Expensive for what is mostly convenience

guides.author: thomas
guides.title: The best bean-to-cup coffee machine
guides.intro: We brewed more than 1,500 cups of coffee with 12 fully automatic bean-to-cup machines. The Bonaro One makes the best espresso in its price range and is the easiest to keep clean.
guides.forWho: A bean-to-cup machine grinds and brews coffee in one step. That’s ideal if you drink several cups a day and want to stop using pods or capsules.
guides.howTested: A panel of five tasters rated espresso, lungo and cappuccino blind. We measured the temperature in the cup, brewing time and how long daily cleaning took.

faq.q: How often should I descale?
faq.a: Depending on water hardness, every one to three months. A water filter extends that period.

faq.q: Which beans work best?
faq.a: Use beans with a matte surface. Shiny, oily beans can clog the grinder.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: Bonaro One
picks.verdict: Brews a full-bodied espresso at 153 °F and has a brew group you rinse under the tap.
cons: Milk foam only via a separate wand

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: Caffino Basic
picks.verdict: A simple machine for people who mostly drink black coffee.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: Bonaro Barista
picks.verdict: Makes milk drinks at the touch of a button and remembers profiles for four users.

guides.author: lauren
guides.title: The best mattress in a box
guides.intro: Four testers each slept for two weeks on 11 mattresses in a box. The Dreamr Hybrid scored best for side and back sleepers.
guides.forWho: You buy a mattress in a box online and can usually try it for 100 nights. That’s a good option if you don’t feel like visiting a showroom.
guides.howTested: Testers of different heights, weights and sleeping positions slept on every mattress. We measured pressure distribution with a pressure mat, edge support and surface temperature.

faq.q: How long should a mattress air out after unboxing?
faq.a: Expect 24 to 48 hours before the mattress reaches full height and the smell is gone.

faq.q: What if I don’t like the mattress?
faq.a: All models in this guide have a trial period of at least 100 nights with free pickup.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: Dreamr Hybrid
picks.verdict: Pocket springs with a layer of high-resilience foam give firm support without pressure points at the shoulders.

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: Slumbr Foam
picks.verdict: An all-foam mattress that’s good enough for back sleepers under 175 lbs.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: Dreamr Hybrid Plus
picks.verdict: With zoned support and a washable cover for people with back or neck pain.
pros: Best pressure relief in the test
cons: On the firm side for light side sleepers

guides.author: sarah
guides.title: The best dehumidifier for a damp home
guides.intro: We tested 9 dehumidifiers in a damp basement and a windowless bathroom. The DryAir 20L pulled the most water out of the air per kWh.
guides.forWho: A dehumidifier helps against condensation, mold and a musty smell. It’s especially useful in a basement, a north-facing bedroom or for drying laundry indoors.
guides.howTested: Each unit ran for 48 hours in the same sealed room. We measured how many liters of water it collected, its power use and the noise on night mode.

faq.q: What humidity level is ideal?
faq.a: Indoors, humidity between 40 and 60 percent is healthy. Above 70 percent, mold grows faster.

faq.q: How much does a dehumidifier cost to run?
faq.a: Our pick used 0.24 kWh per hour on average. Eight hours a day, that’s about $10 a month at $0.17 per kWh.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: DryAir 20L
picks.verdict: Collects 14 liters a day while using less power than most smaller models.

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: Aqua Stop 12
picks.verdict: Enough for a bathroom or a small bedroom.
cons: Too little capacity for a basement

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: DryAir 30 Pro
picks.verdict: With a drain hose connection, so it can run day and night.
cons: Loud on the highest setting: 52 dB

guides.author: lauren
guides.title: The best electric lawn mower
guides.intro: We spent eight weeks mowing three different lawns with 10 electric mowers. The GreenEdge 37 Cordless cuts the cleanest and covers 3,200 sq ft on one battery.
guides.forWho: A cordless mower is quiet, starts instantly and needs less maintenance than a gas mower. For yards up to about 5,400 sq ft it’s more than enough.
guides.howTested: We mowed short and long grass, wet and dry, on flat and sloped lawns. We measured runtime per battery, noise and how well the grass bag filled.

faq.q: How long does a battery last?
faq.a: A lithium-ion battery lasts 500 to 800 charge cycles on average. For most yards, that’s five to eight years.

faq.q: Can I mow wet grass?
faq.a: You can, but the result looks worse and the bag clogs faster.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: GreenEdge 37 Cordless
picks.verdict: Cuts evenly, even in long grass, and has a grass bag that fills to the last blade.
pros: Battery fits the brand’s other tools

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: MowMate 32
picks.verdict: A good, light choice for a small city yard.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: GreenEdge 46 Pro
picks.verdict: Two batteries and an 18-inch cutting width for large lawns.
pros: Covers 6,500 sq ft on one charge

guides.author: jake
guides.title: The best cordless drill for home use
guides.intro: We drilled more than 600 holes in wood, steel and masonry with 13 cordless drills. The Torq 18V is powerful enough for any job around the house and feels great in the hand.
guides.forWho: You use a cordless drill for driving screws, holes in wood and metal, and light masonry work. For concrete you need a rotary hammer.
guides.howTested: We drove 100 screws of 5 × 60 mm into pine and drilled holes in steel and brick. We measured how many screws each battery handled and how hot the tool got.

faq.q: What’s the difference between a drill and a driver?
faq.a: A driver has a clutch that stops when the screw is tight. Most cordless drills combine both.

faq.q: How many volts do I need?
faq.a: For jobs around the house, 12 volts is enough. Choose 18 volts if you often drill into hardwood or masonry.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: Torq 18V
picks.verdict: Drives 100 screws on one battery and has a clutch that engages precisely.

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: Boorix Start
picks.verdict: Good enough for assembling furniture and the occasional shelf.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: Torq 18V Brushless
picks.verdict: Brushless motor with hammer mode that drills an 8 mm hole even in masonry.

guides.author: jake
guides.title: The best smart thermostat
guides.intro: We installed 8 smart thermostats in three homes with furnaces and heat pumps. The WarmWise 3 saved the most energy without sacrificing comfort.
guides.forWho: A smart thermostat adjusts the temperature to when you’re home. It saves the most if you have irregular working hours.
guides.howTested: We installed each thermostat ourselves and tracked energy use for twelve weeks, compared with a regular programmable thermostat. We also tested the app and integration with Google, Alexa and HomeKit.

faq.q: Does a smart thermostat work with every HVAC system?
faq.a: Almost all modern systems work with it. Some models need a C-wire for continuous power.

faq.q: How much do you really save?
faq.a: In our test, between 6 and 11 percent on energy compared with a programmable thermostat, depending on how often you’re away.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: WarmWise 3
picks.verdict: Controls the furnace with modulation and saved 11 percent on energy in our test.
pros: Works with all major smart home platforms

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: Thermi Go
picks.verdict: A simple smart thermostat with a clear app and no subscription.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: WarmWise Pro
picks.verdict: Also works with a heat pump and controls each room with separate vent sensors.

guides.author: lauren
guides.title: The best baby monitor
guides.intro: Three families used 9 baby monitors for six weeks. The Hush Cam 2 has the clearest night vision and the most reliable range.
guides.forWho: A baby monitor lets you hear or see when your child wakes up. A model with its own parent unit also works without Wi-Fi, which many parents prefer.
guides.howTested: We tested range through walls and floors, parent unit battery life, audio and video delay, and night vision quality.

faq.q: Is a Wi-Fi baby monitor safe?
faq.a: It can be, if the manufacturer offers encryption and two-factor authentication. A model with its own parent unit doesn’t connect to the internet.

faq.q: How far does a baby monitor reach?
faq.a: Manufacturers often state 1,000 feet in open space. Indoors, the models in our test reached 80 to 200 feet.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: Hush Cam 2
picks.verdict: Sharp night vision and a range that reached into the backyard in our test house.
pros: Works without Wi-Fi or an app
cons: 4.3-inch screen is on the small side

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: BabyEar Audio
picks.verdict: Audio only, but clear, with a light that turns on with sound.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: Hush Cam Pro
picks.verdict: Pan-and-tilt camera with temperature sensor and a bigger screen.

guides.author: sarah
guides.title: The best washing machine of 2026
guides.intro: We ran more than 400 loads with 12 washing machines. The CleanWash 8 removes the most stains on cold and is efficient with water and power.
guides.photoNote: washing machines in a laundry room
guides.forWho: This guide is for anyone looking for a front-loader for a household of two to five people.
guides.howTested: Each machine washed stain strips with wine, grass, blood and makeup on cold and warm. We measured water and power use per cycle, remaining moisture after the spin cycle and noise.

faq.q: Is washing on cold clean enough?
faq.a: For most laundry, yes. In our test, our pick removed 94 percent of stains on cold. Wash towels and bedding on hot every now and then.

faq.q: What capacity do I need?
faq.a: For two people, a standard drum is enough; for a family of four, choose a large-capacity model.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: CleanWash 8
picks.verdict: Best cleaning on cold and the lowest power use of all machines tested.
pros: ENERGY STAR certified, measured 0.48 kWh per load

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: Drum Basic 7
picks.verdict: A solid machine without bells and whistles for a small household.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: CleanWash 9 Pro
picks.verdict: With a steam cycle and a motor the manufacturer warrants for ten years.

guides.author: lauren
guides.title: The best electric toothbrush
guides.intro: A panel of ten testers brushed for eight weeks with 15 electric toothbrushes, checked by a dental hygienist. The Gleam Sonic 5 removed the most plaque.
guides.forWho: In studies, an electric toothbrush removes more plaque than a manual one. This guide helps you choose between sonic and oscillating models.
guides.howTested: A dental hygienist measured the amount of plaque with a disclosing agent before and after each test period. We also rated battery life, the timer, pressure control and the price of replacement heads.

faq.q: How often should I replace the brush head?
faq.a: Every three months, or sooner if the bristles start to splay.

faq.q: Sonic or oscillating?
faq.a: In our test the difference was small. Choose mainly on brush head price and whether you want pressure control.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: Gleam Sonic 5
picks.verdict: Removed the most plaque and warns you when you press too hard.

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: Brushly One
picks.verdict: A simple brush with a timer that already cleans much better than a manual toothbrush.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: Gleam Sonic 9
picks.verdict: With an app that shows which teeth you skip and a travel case that charges the brush.
cons: App adds little for most people

guides.author: sarah
guides.title: The best automatic cat feeder
guides.intro: Our test cats ate from 8 automatic feeders for six weeks. The Kibbly Timer 4 delivered the most accurate portions and kept working when the Wi-Fi went down.
guides.forWho: An automatic feeder is handy if your cat needs small portions at set times, or if you’re away for a day. For longer than a day, we always recommend a pet sitter.
guides.howTested: We weighed every portion to measure accuracy, tested what happened during a power or Wi-Fi outage, and checked whether our cats could break into the feeder.

faq.q: Can my cat break into an automatic feeder?
faq.a: With three of the eight models, our cats managed to get to the food supply. Our pick has a locking lid.

faq.q: How long can I leave my cat alone with an automatic feeder?
faq.a: One day at most. A cat also needs fresh water, a clean litter box and attention.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: Kibbly Timer 4
picks.verdict: Portions are off by only 2 grams on average, and it runs on batteries during a power outage.

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: FeedClock Mini
picks.verdict: A simple timer with two compartments for wet food with an ice pack.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: Kibbly Cam
picks.verdict: With a camera, so you can see whether your cat has eaten.
cons: Only works with an app and account

guides.author: jake
guides.title: The best video doorbell without a subscription
guides.intro: We mounted 10 video doorbells next to our front door for eight weeks. The RingWise 2K has the sharpest image and stores recordings locally, with no monthly fees.
guides.photoNote: video doorbells by a front door
guides.forWho: A video doorbell shows you on your phone who’s at the door, even when you’re not home. Handy for package deliveries and if you’re away often.
guides.howTested: We measured the delay between the ring and the notification, rated the image by day and by night, and checked how recordings are stored and secured. We also checked that the camera doesn’t film too much of the street.

faq.q: Can I film the sidewalk with a video doorbell?
faq.a: Laws vary by state, but recording public areas is generally allowed while recording audio may require consent. Set privacy zones to block out neighbors and the street.

faq.q: Do I need a subscription?
faq.a: Not with the models in this guide. They store recordings locally.

picks.label: Our pick
picks.name: RingWise 2K
picks.verdict: Sharp image, fast alerts and local storage on a microSD card.

picks.label: Budget pick
picks.name: Belcam Lite
picks.verdict: Cheap and simple, with a fine image during the day.

picks.label: Upgrade
picks.name: RingWise Pro
picks.verdict: Wired, with facial recognition that runs entirely on the device.

info.title: Editorial guidelines
info.lead: These rules apply to every buying guide and review on HouseholdMe.

sections.heading: Independent judgment
sections.body: Only the editorial team decides which products we recommend. Manufacturers and retailers cannot pay for a spot, a higher score or a positive mention.

sections.heading: Tested ourselves
sections.body: We only recommend products we have used ourselves. Every guide states how many models we tested, for how long, and who ran the test.

sections.heading: Reviewed by the editor-in-chief
sections.body: Before publication, every buying guide is checked by the editor-in-chief for facts, measurements and sources.

sections.heading: Kept up to date
sections.body: We review every buying guide at least four times a year. Changes are listed at the bottom of the article with a date.

sections.heading: Use of AI
sections.body: Our articles are written by our testers. We do not use AI to generate test results or verdicts.

info.title: How we make money
info.lead: HouseholdMe is free to read. We make money through affiliate links.

sections.heading: What is an affiliate link?
sections.body: When you go from a store button on our site to a retailer and buy something there, that retailer pays us a small commission. You don’t pay anything extra.

sections.heading: Which retailers do we work with?
sections.body: Among others, Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart and Target. We only show a retailer if it has the product in stock at a reasonable price.

sections.heading: What we don’t do
sections.body: We don’t run manufacturer ads, write sponsored articles or accept payment for a review.

sections.heading: How do you recognize an affiliate link?
sections.body: All store buttons on our site are affiliate links. A notice at the top of every article explains this.

info.title: Corrections policy
info.lead: We sometimes make mistakes. Here’s how we handle them.

sections.heading: Report an error
sections.body: Email corrections@householdme.com with a link to the article and a description of the error.

sections.heading: What we do
sections.body: We respond within two business days. If the report is correct, we update the article.

sections.heading: Transparency
sections.body: Substantive corrections are listed at the bottom of the article, with a date and a short description of what changed.

info.title: Privacy & cookies
info.lead: We collect as little data as possible.

sections.heading: What data
sections.body: We use analytics cookies without storing your full IP address. If you sign up for the newsletter, we store your email address.

sections.heading: Affiliate cookies
sections.body: When you click a store button, the retailer or affiliate network sets a cookie to record that you came from us. We ask for your consent for this.

sections.heading: Your rights
sections.body: You can always ask what data we hold about you and have it deleted. Email privacy@householdme.com.

sections.heading: Information
sections.body: We do our best to keep all information accurate and up to date. Prices and availability at retailers may change.

sections.heading: Purchases
sections.body: You don’t buy from HouseholdMe but from the retailer. The retailer’s terms apply to delivery, warranty and returns.

sections.heading: Copyright
sections.body: Text, photos and measurements on this site are the property of HouseholdMe Media LLC. You may only reuse them with attribution and a link.
